subject: religious-studies
title: The Problem of Evil and Religious Experience
welcome_lead: Confront the most painful question in philosophy of religion and survey the experiential evidence offered in reply.
meta_desc: A-Level Religious Studies adventure on the problem of evil, Augustinian and Irenaean theodicies, and religious experience.
final_note: You have explored two classical theodicies, Plantinga's free-will defence, and the role of experience in theistic belief.

walkthroughs.body_html: J. L. Mackie's 'Evil and Omnipotence' (1955) argued the omnipotent, wholly good God is logically incompatible with any evil. Alvin Plantinga's The Nature of Necessity (1974) replied that a world with free creatures who sometimes choose evil may be better than any world without them, and is possible. William Rowe shifted ground to evidential arguments using cases like fawn suffering in a forest fire.

Augustine, in Confessions VII and City of God XI-XIV, treats evil as privatio boni, a lack of due good, originating in angelic and human misuse of free will. John Hick's Evil and the God of Love (1966) drew on Irenaeus to argue God places humans at an 'epistemic distance' in a soul-making environment, eventually leading all to mature in the divine image.

Richard Swinburne's The Existence of God (1979) treats religious experience under the Principles of Credulity and Testimony as adding probabilistic weight to theism. William James's Varieties (1902) catalogues mystical experiences across traditions. Critics from Freud to Persinger offer psychological or neurological explanations; defenders reply that explaining is not explaining away.

mcqs.q: What distinction matters for the free will defence to the problem of evil?
options: Natural evil means evil that is good for nature.
The free will defence solves all forms of evil at once.
It is the question of whether the devil really exists.

Between moral evil (caused by free human choices) and natural evil (earthquakes, disease) — the free will defence directly addresses moral evil but struggles with natural evil, which isn't a product of free choice.

mcqs.q: What is the problem of evil?
options: Natural evil means evil that is good for nature.
If God is all-loving, all-knowing and all-powerful, why does evil and suffering exist? Logically, all four cannot be true together without explanation.
It is the question of whether evil people will go to hell.
It is the question of whether the devil really exists.

Five distinct arguments for God's existence: from motion, causation, contingency, gradation of being, and final causes/teleology — collectively forming Aquinas's natural theology, not a single argument.
Aquinas's Five Ways are five Christian sacraments.
Natural evil means evil that is good for nature.
Aquinas's Five Ways are five steps of one cosmological argument.
